name: Executive Order of February 11, 1887 setting apart the present Jicarilla Apache reservation (Royce 691)
citation: Executive Order of February 11, 1887 (Royce; the Commission's 1966 opinion gives February 11, its 1963 Finding 56 gives February 1)
promises: Not a treaty. The President set apart lands in New Mexico (Townships 27 to 30 North in Ranges 1 East and 1 to 3 West, and more) as a reservation for the Jicarilla Apache, except rights any bona fide settler had acquired by actual settlement (Royce).
The Commission found this reservation was virtually the same as the one created in 1880, that the Jicarilla moved onto it in 1887 and have lived there since.

breaches.what: The Commission found that, through settlers, the military and other agents, the United States gradually deprived the Jicarilla of their aboriginal title without payment, moving them from one reservation to another until the final move onto this reservation in 1887.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Jicarilla Apache Tribe v. United States, Docket 22-A, Findings of Fact and Interlocutory Order of August 26, 1963 (12 Ind. Cl. Comm. 439)

breaches.what: The Commission fixed the date of taking as August 20, 1883, when the military began removing the Jicarilla to Fort Stanton, and held the tribe entitled to the fair market value of 9,218,532.77 acres outside the confirmed Spanish and Mexican land grants.

landTaken: The Royce 691 area is the reservation the Jicarilla kept. The taking found by the Commission is of the aboriginal land around it: 9,218,532.77 acres valued (Docket 22-A, 1966).
today: The Jicarilla Apache Nation still lives on this reservation. The Docket 22-A taking is counted once, under cession-1886-10-01-apache-eastern-bands.

openQuestions: This order gave the Jicarilla land; the breach is the Docket 22-A taking of the land around it, ending in confinement here. That taking is already recorded under cession-1886-10-01-apache-eastern-bands, so this file is marked sameEventAs that record.
Order date: Royce prints February 11, 1887; Docket 22-A Finding 56 (1963) says February 1, 1887; the 1966 opinion says February 11. February 11 is used.
The Jicarilla accounting claim (Docket 22-K) was settled in 1974 and is not researched here.
The Jicarilla Apache Nation's own account of 1887 was not located.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. In 1887 the President set apart the present Jicarilla Apache reservation in New Mexico, where the people have lived since.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found the United States had taken the Jicarilla's much larger homeland without payment, dating the taking to the 1883 removal to Fort Stanton.
plain.today: The claim was settled in 1971 for $9,150,000. The taking is counted once, under the Eastern Apache record.
